items.sentence_raw: The role of governments in environmental management is difficult but inescapable.
items.explain:
Q14: The first sentence of Section A says *'The role of governments in environmental management is difficult but inescapable'* — this is a general statement about **governments** and **management of the environment**. So the heading that matches is **v**.

Q28: The whole passage discusses how governments affect the environment through policies like subsidies, starting with *'The role of governments in environmental management is difficult but inescapable'*. The main topic is **environmental management**. So the answer is **A**.

items.sentence_raw: Sometimes, the state tries to manage the resources it owns, and does so badly.
Often, however, governments act in an even more harmful way.
They actually subsidise the exploitation and consumption of natural resources.
A whole range of policies, from farm price support to protection for coal-mining, do environmental damage and (often) make no economic sense.
Scrapping them offers a two-fold bonus: a cleaner environment and a more efficient economy.
Growth and environmentalism can actually go hand in hand, if politicians have the courage to confront the vested interest that subsidies create.
No activity affects more of the earth's surface than farming.
items.explain: Q15: Section B starts with *'No activity affects more of the earth's surface than farming'* and then talks about *'World food output per head has risen'*. This section connects **farming** with **food output**. So the correct heading is **vii**.

items.sentence_raw: It shapes a third of the planet's land area, not counting Antarctica, and the proportion is rising.

World food output per head has risen by 4 per cent between the 1970s and 1980s mainly as a result of increases in yields from land already in cultivation, but also because more land has been brought under the plough.
items.explain: Q15: Section B starts with *'No activity affects more of the earth's surface than farming'* and then talks about *'World food output per head has risen'*. This section connects **farming** with **food output**. So the correct heading is **vii**.

items.sentence_raw: Higher yields have been achieved by increased irrigation, better crop breeding, and a doubling in the use of pesticides and chemical fertilisers in the 1970s and 1980s.
All these activities may have damaging environmental impacts.

For example, land clearing for agriculture is the largest single cause of deforestation; chemical fertilisers and pesticides may contaminate water supplies; more intensive farming and the abandonment of fallow periods tend to exacerbate soil erosion; and the spread of monoculture and use of high-yielding varieties of crops have been accompanied by the disappearance of old varieties of food plants which might have provided some insurance against pests or diseases in future.
items.explain:
Q16: Section C gives examples like *'land clearing for agriculture is the largest single cause of deforestation'* and *'chemical fertilisers and pesticides may contaminate water supplies'*. All these are **environmental impacts** of **modern farming**. So the heading is **ii**.

Q19: The passage says *'land clearing for agriculture is the largest single cause of deforestation'* — **'land clearing'** is the agricultural practice, and **'deforestation'** is the environmental damage. So the answer is **G**.

Q20: The passage says *'chemical fertilisers and pesticides may contaminate water supplies'* — **'chemical fertilisers and pesticides'** are **chemical inputs**, and **'contaminate water supplies'** means **degraded water supply**. So the answer is **C**.

Q21: The passage says *'more intensive farming and the abandonment of fallow periods tend to exacerbate soil erosion'* — **'more intensive farming'** leads to **'soil erosion'**. So the answer is **F**.

Q22: The passage says *'the spread of monoculture... have been accompanied by the disappearance of old varieties of food plants'* — **'expansion of monoculture'** leads to **'disappearance of old plant varieties'**. So the answer is **B**.

items.sentence_raw: Soil erosion threatens the productivity of land In both rich and poor countries.
The United States, where the most careful measurements have been done, discovered in 1982 that about one-fifth of its farmland was losing topsoil at a rate likely to diminish the soil's productivity.
items.explain: Q23: The passage says the US discovered in 1982 that *'about one-fifth of its farmland was losing topsoil at a rate likely to diminish the soil's productivity'* — **'one-fifth'** means **20 per cent**, and it was **causing significant damage**. So the answer is **C**.

items.sentence_raw: The country subsequently embarked upon a program to convert 11 per cent of its cropped land to meadow or forest.
Topsoil in India and China is vanishing much faster than in America.
Government policies have frequently compounded the environmental damage that farming can cause.
items.explain: Q17: Section D begins with *'Government policies have frequently compounded the environmental damage that farming can cause'* and then gives examples from **rich countries** like Denmark and the Netherlands. So the heading is **iv**.

items.sentence_raw: In the rich countries, subsidies for growing crops and price supports for farm output drive up the price of land.
The annual value of these subsidies is immense: about $250 billion, or more than all World Bank lending in the 1980s.
To increase the output of crops per acre, a farmer's easiest option is to use more of the most readily available inputs: fertilisers and pesticides.
Fertiliser use doubled in Denmark in the period 1960-1985 and increased in The Netherlands by 150 per cent.
items.explain: Q24: The passage says *'Fertiliser use doubled in Denmark in the period 1960-1985'* — **'doubled'** means they **used twice as much** as before. So the answer is **B**.

items.sentence_raw: The quantity of pesticides applied has risen too; by 69 per cent In 1975-1984 in Denmark, for example, with a rise of 115 per cent in the frequency of application in the three years from 1981.
In the late 1980s and early 1990s some efforts were made to reduce farm subsidies.
The most dramatic example was that of New Zealand, which scrapped most farm support in 1984.

A study of the environmental effects, conducted in 1993, found that the end of fertiliser subsidies had been followed by a fall in fertiliser use (a fall compounded by the decline in world commodity prices, which cut farm incomes).
The removal of subsidies also stopped land-clearing and over-stocking, which in the past had been the principal causes of erosion.
Farms began to diversify.
items.explain: Q25: The passage says that after subsidies were removed in New Zealand, *'Farms began to diversify'* — this is a direct match for **farm diversification**. So the answer is **D**.

items.sentence_raw: The one kind of subsidy whose removal appeared to have been bad for the environment was the subsidy to manage soil erosion, In less enlightened countries, and in the European Union, the trend has been to reduce rather than eliminate subsidies, and to introduce new payments to encourage farmers to treat their land In environmentally friendlier ways, or to leave it fallow.
items.explain: Q26: The passage says *'In less enlightened countries... the trend has been to reduce rather than eliminate subsidies'* — this means their policies do not see the **long-term benefit of ending subsidies** completely, unlike New Zealand. So the answer is **C**.

items.sentence_raw: It may sound strange but such payments need to be higher than the existing incentives for farmers to grow food crops.
Farmers, however, dislike being paid to do nothing.

In several countries they have become interested in the possibility of using fuel produced from crop residues either as a replacement for petrol (as ethanol) or as fuel for power stations (as biomass).
Such fuels produce far less carbon dioxide than coal or oil, and absorb carbon dioxide as they grow.
They are therefore less likely to contribute to the greenhouse effect.
But they die rarely competitive with fossil fuels unless subsidised - and growing them does no less environmental harm than other crops.
In poor countries, governments aggravate other sorts of damage.
Subsidies for pesticides and artificial fertilisers encourage farmers to use greater quantities than are needed to get the highest economic crop yield.

A study by the International Rice Research Institute Of pesticide use by farmers in South East Asia found that, with pest-resistant varieties of rice, even moderate applications of pesticide frequently cost farmers more than they saved.
Such waste puts farmers on a chemical treadmill: bugs and weeds become resistant to poisons, so next year's poisons must be more lethal.
One cost is to human health, Every year some 10,000 people die from pesticide poisoning, almost all of them in the developing countries, and another 400,000 become seriously ill.
As for artificial fertilisers, their use world-wide increased by 40 per cent per unit of farmed land between the mid 1970s and late 1980s, mostly in the developing countries.
Overuse of fertilisers may cause farmers to stop rotating crops or leaving their land fallow.
That, In turn, may make soil erosion worse.
A result of the Uruguay Round of world trade negotiations Is likely to be a reduction of 36 per cent In the average levels of farm subsidies paid by the rich countries in 1986-1990.
items.explain: Q18: Section F talks about *'A result of the Uruguay Round of world trade negotiations'* and its likely effects on farm subsidies. This is about the **probable effects** of a **new international trade agreement**. So the heading is **i**.

items.sentence_raw: Some of the world's food production will move from Western Europe to regions where subsidies are lower or non-existent, such as the former communist countries and parts of the developing world.
Some environmentalists worry about this outcome.
It will undoubtedly mean more pressure to convert natural habitat into farmland.
But it will also have many desirable environmental effects.
The intensity of farming in the rich world should decline, and the use of chemical inputs will diminish.
Crops are more likely to be grown in the environments to which they are naturally suited.
And more farmers in poor countries wilt have the money and the incentive to manage their land in ways that are sustainable in the long run.
items.explain: Q27: The passage says the Uruguay Round means *'more farmers in poor countries will have the money and the incentive to manage their land in ways that are sustainable in the long run'* — this directly supports **more sustainable farming practices**. So the answer is **A**.

items.sentence_raw: That is important.
To feed an increasingly hungry world, farmers need every incentive to use their soil and water effectively and efficiently.
